claims.text: A DFT-based ab initio free-energy method using thermodynamic integration and two-phase coexistence simulations can accurately calculate the melting temperature of high-melting refractory materials.
The method can calculate the entropy of fusion.
The method can calculate the enthalpy of fusion.
The method can calculate the volume change at the melting point.
The initial material is a crystalline, high-melting refractory solid at ambient or moderate temperature.
Refractory high-entropy alloys have extremely high melting points.
Thermodynamic integration computes the free-energy difference between solid and liquid phases.
Thermodynamic integration tracks a gradual free-energy change between solid and liquid states.
The melting temperature is identified when the free energies of the solid and liquid phases are equal.
Entropy and enthalpy changes at fusion can be derived from the free-energy treatment.
The volume difference between phases at melting can be derived from the proposed treatment.
With appropriately chosen DFT parameters, the calculated melting properties should closely agree with experiments or high-accuracy benchmarks.
Experimental measurement of refractory-material melting properties is challenging because of the high melting temperatures.
The proposed method has high computational expense.
Predicted melting properties are sensitive to the selected DFT exchange-correlation functional and simulation parameters.
Uncertainty in DFT and simulation choices may affect absolute predicted values while leaving trends reliable.
Despite variation in numerical agreement with experiment, the method should reliably capture key trends and relative differences.
